title: Writing Poetry
keyIdea: A poem is words that sound good together. Rhyming words end with the same sound, like bus and fuss, or high and sky. Two lines that rhyme make a couplet. Clap the beats in a line: el-e-phants is 3 claps, not 1. A pattern poem repeats the start of each line and changes the end. When you say a poem aloud, let the words tell your voice to be loud, soft, fast or slow.

kid: A poem plays with the sound of words. Say cat, mat, hat. They end the same. That is a rhyme. Two lines that end in a rhyme make a couplet: I see a big red bus. It makes a lot of fuss.

Words that start the same do not rhyme. Bus and bell both start with b, but the ends are not the same. Listen to the end of the word, not the start. High and sky rhyme, but they are spelt in different ways.

Poems have a beat. Clap once for each beat as you say a line. Hop, hop, hop is 3 claps. A long word can get more than one clap: el-e-phants is 3. Lines that go together sound best with the same claps.

Some poems use a pattern. Each line starts the same, like I can hear, and ends in a new way: the bees buzz, the rain drips. Then say your poem out loud. Shh means soft. Big letters mean loud. Creeps slowly means slow.
adult: In England, Year 2 pupils write poetry and learn poems by heart, reciting them with appropriate intonation so the meaning is clear (National Curriculum, KS1). The US standards ask the same age to describe how words and phrases, such as regular beats, alliteration, rhymes and repeated lines, supply rhythm and meaning in a poem or song (CCSS RL.2.4).

Three tools carry most early poems. Rhyme is a match of the final vowel sound and everything after it, the rime (c-at, m-at); a rhyming couplet is two lines that end in a rhyme. Rhythm is the pattern of beats, and at this age a clap per syllable is the working measure. Repetition, such as a repeated opening, gives a pattern poem its shape and helps children remember it.

Common mistakes: treating words that start alike as rhymes (bus and bell are alliteration), judging rhyme by spelling rather than sound (high and sky rhyme; cough and dough do not), giving a long word a single clap, ending a pattern by copying a whole earlier line, and reciting every line in the same flat voice.

In the lab your child finishes three couplets with a rhyme, matches the claps of two lines, adds lines to an I can hear pattern poem, and picks a loud, soft, fast or slow voice from clues in the words. Every drag has a big button twin.

familyTip: Make an I can hear poem together on a walk or at the window. Each of you adds a line that starts I can hear. Then clap the beats of one line, and read the whole poem once in a whisper and once in a big voice.

visual.caption: Does it rhyme with cat? Drag each word to a box, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: finish couplets with a rhyme, match the claps of two lines, keep a pattern poem going, and pick the voice that fits the words.

practice.hint: Say the words and listen to the end sound.
practice.explain: Tree and bee end with the same ee sound. Tray starts like tree, but it ends in a different way.

practice.prompt: Mia writes {a} rhyming couplets. A couplet is 2 lines. How many lines does she write?
practice.hint: Each couplet has 2 lines. Count 2 for each one.
practice.explain: {a} couplets with 2 lines each make {=2*a} lines.

practice.hint: Say it slowly and clap each beat: di … no … saur.
practice.explain: Di-no-saur has 3 beats, so 3 claps. Clap the beats, not the letters.

practice.prompt: A poem has {a} lines. Each line has {b} claps. How many claps in the whole poem?
practice.hint: Add the claps for each line. Every line has the same number.
practice.explain: {a} lines with {b} claps each make {=a*b} claps in the poem.

pool.hint: Look for two words that end the same way.
pool.explain: Night and light end with the same ite sound. The other pairs only start the same.

pool.prompt: Finish the couplet: “I have a little boat. / I hope that it will …”
pool.explain: Boat and float rhyme, so the two lines make a couplet.

pool.prompt: A poem goes: “I can see a red bus. I can see a blue car.” Which line keeps the pattern?
choices: I can see a green van.
I can see a red bus.
pool.hint: Keep the start the same, but say something new.
pool.explain: “I can see a green van” keeps the start I can see and adds a new thing.

pool.prompt: How should you read “BANG! went the drum”?
pool.hint: Look at the big letters and the !.
pool.explain: BANG in big letters with an ! tells you to read it loudly.

choices: One is a thing you ride
pool.hint: Where do rhyming words match: at the start or at the end?
pool.explain: Rhymes match at the end. Bus and bell only share the b at the start.

pool.prompt: Which line has the same claps as “Hot red sun” (3 claps)?
choices: Lots of white snow on the hill
pool.explain: Cold white snow is 3 claps, the same as hot red sun.

pool.prompt: Sam’s pattern poem has {a} lines. He adds {b} more lines that start “I can hear”. How many lines now?
pool.hint: Start with the lines he has and add the new ones.
pool.explain: {a} lines and {b} more make {=a+b} lines in his poem.

pool.prompt: A couplet ends with a pair of rhyming words. Zoe writes {a} couplets. How many rhyming words are at the line ends?
pool.hint: Each couplet ends with a pair of rhyming words.
pool.explain: {a} couplets each end with 2 rhyming words, so {=2*a} words.

pool.prompt: Which two words rhyme even though they are spelt in a different way?
pool.hint: Say them. Listen, do not just look.
pool.explain: Blue and shoe both end with the oo sound, so they rhyme. Rhyme is about sound, not spelling.
